items.q: Why is reading array[500] just as fast as reading array[0] in an array?
options: The computer is just very fast, so order doesn't matter
Arrays secretly keep a copy of every element at position 0
It isn't — array[500] must scan past the first 500 elements
Elements are stored contiguously and the same size, so the location is computed directly (start + index x size)

explain.right: Contiguous, equal-size elements let the computer calculate the exact address and jump there, so indexing is O(1) regardless of position.
explain.wrong: Indexing doesn't scan earlier elements, and there's no hidden copy; the address math is what makes it constant time.

items.q: In a Python list (a dynamic array), which operation is O(n) because elements must shift?
options: Inserting at the front with insert(0, x)

explain.right: Inserting at the front forces every later element to shift over to stay contiguous, which is O(n).
explain.wrong: Index reads and length checks are O(1), and appending to the end is amortized O(1) (no shifting needed).

items.q: Compared with an array, a linked list trades which costs?
options: It is strictly better at everything
It uses less memory and is more cache-friendly
Cheaper insert/delete at a known node (O(1)) but slower indexing (O(n), you must walk the chain)

explain.right: Linked-list nodes splice cheaply once you're there, but reaching the i-th element means following links from the start, so indexing is O(n).
explain.wrong: It's not strictly better; it uses more memory (pointers) and is less cache-friendly, and indexing is its weak point.

items.q: A Python list (or JavaScript array) is implemented as which structure?
options: A dynamic array (a resizable contiguous block)

explain.right: Python lists and JS arrays are dynamic arrays: contiguous blocks that grow by copying into a larger block, which is why indexing and append are fast.
explain.wrong: They're not linked lists, maps, or trees; assuming 'list' means linked list is a common mix-up that predicts the wrong costs.

items.q: You need a collection where you mostly append and frequently read by index. Array-style list or linked list, and why?
rubric: Justifies with O(1) index access (and amortized O(1) append)
Notes the linked list's O(n) indexing makes it a poor fit here

explain.right: Strong answers pick the dynamic array for O(1) indexing and cheap appends, and note linked-list indexing is O(n).
explain.wrong: A weak answer picks the linked list for 'flexibility' without accounting for the O(n) index cost that dominates this workload.
